summary.title: Visualization of π-hole in molecules by means of Kelvin probe force microscopy
summary.authors: B Mallada, M Ondráček, M Lamanec, A Gallardo, A Jiménez-Martín, B De La Torre, P Hobza, P Jelínek
summary.executive_summary: This study presents the first direct experimental visualization of the π-hole, a submolecular charge distribution feature in halogen-substituted polyaromatic hydrocarbons, using Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM). While the existence of π-holes has been theoretically predicted and indirectly inferred from spectroscopic data, direct real-space observation has remained elusive. The authors investigate 9,10-Dichlorooctafluoroanthracene (FCl-An) and anthracene (An) self-assembled on an Au(111) surface. Using non-contact atomic force microscopy (nc-AFM) to resolve molecular structures, they demonstrate that FCl-An molecules exhibit a distinct bow-tie pattern in the local contact potential difference (LCPD) maps, corresponding to the π-electron-deficient cavity. In contrast, anthracene lacks this feature. The study further elucidates the impact of the π-hole on molecular adsorption. Force-distance spectroscopy reveals that FCl-An adsorbs at a greater height (360 pm) compared to anthracene (330 pm) on the Au(111) surface. Theoretical calculations, including DFT and SAPT0, indicate that the π-hole increases the ionization potential of FCl-An, thereby suppressing charge density induction at the molecule-metal interface. This reduction in induced electrostatic interactions leads to weaker adsorption and a higher adsorption height. The work confirms that the π-hole significantly modulates non-covalent interactions, specifically affecting the electrostatic component of molecule-surface binding. By combining high-resolution imaging with theoretical modeling, the paper establishes KPFM as a powerful tool for mapping submolecular charge distributions and understanding their role in physical-chemical properties. The findings expand the understanding of π-hole systems and open avenues for studying how internal charge distributions influence molecular interactions and stability in supramolecular assemblies.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study presents the first direct experimental visualization of the π-hole, a submolecular charge distribution feature in halogen-substituted polyaromatic hydrocarbons, using Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM). While the existence of π-holes has been theoretically predicted and indirectly inferred from spectroscopic data, direct real-space observation has remained elusive. The authors investigate 9,10-Dichlorooctafluoroanthracene (FCl-An) and anthracene (An) self-assembled on an Au(111) surface. Using non-contact atomic force microscopy (nc-AFM) to resolve molecular structures, they demonstrate that FCl-An molecules exhibit a distinct bow-tie pattern in the local contact potential difference (LCPD) maps, corresponding to the π-electron-deficient cavity. In contrast, anthracene lacks this feature. The study further elucidates the impact of the π-hole on molecular adsorption. Force-distance spectroscopy reveals that FCl-An adsorbs at a greater height (360 pm) compared to anthracene (330 pm) on the Au(111) surface. Theoretical calculations, including DFT and SAPT0, indicate that the π-hole increases the ionization potential of FCl-An, thereby suppressing charge density induction at the molecule-metal interface. This reduction in induced electrostatic interactions leads to weaker adsorption and a higher adsorption height. The work confirms that the π-hole significantly modulates non-covalent interactions, specifically affecting the electrostatic component of molecule-surface binding. By combining high-resolution imaging with theoretical modeling, the paper establishes KPFM as a powerful tool for mapping submolecular charge distributions and understanding their role in physical-chemical properties. The findings expand the understanding of π-hole systems and open avenues for studying how internal charge distributions influence molecular interactions and stability in supramolecular assemblies.

Research Context
Non-covalent interactions are crucial in chemical and biological processes. The nature of these bonds is determined by dispersion and electrostatic forces. Electrostatic components are highly directional and linked to internal charge distribution. In polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, carbon electronegativity creates electron-rich π-bonds. Substituting hydrogens with electronegative atoms reverses electron population. This creates a π-electron-deficient cavity known as a π-hole. The presence of π-holes affects non-covalent intermolecular interactions. Previously, π-hole existence was proven only indirectly via measured data. Direct experimental observation of π-holes was lacking. Scanning probe microscopy is the most appropriate tool for visualization. KPFM has previously resolved sigma-holes with atomic resolution.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to experimentally confirm the existence of the π-hole. It specifically investigates 9,10-Dichlorooctafluoroanthracene (FCl-An) and anthracene (An). The hypothesis is that FCl-An possesses a π-hole while An does not. The presence of different substituents rules charge transfer between orbitals. Molecular orbitals in FCl-An extend to halogen substituents. This extension gives rise to a π-hole on the carbon skeleton. The study also hypothesizes that π-holes affect adsorption on surfaces. It predicts that the π-hole influences electrostatic interactions with the substrate. The expected outcome is a measurable difference in adsorption height. The π-hole is predicted to increase ionization potential. This should suppress charge density induction at the interface.

Methodological Details
Experiments were conducted at 4.2 K using a Createc STM/nc-AFM microscope. Pt/Ir tips were sharpened by focused ion beam and cleaned. A qPlus sensor with 30 kHz frequency was used for nc-AFM. The Au(111) substrate was prepared by Ar+ sputtering and annealing. FCl-An and An were sublimated simultaneously in UHV at room temperature. Molecular self-assemblies were formed on the Au(111) surface. STM images were acquired at a base temperature of 4.8 K. nc-AFM used a functionalized carbon monoxide (CO) tip. KPFM recorded spatial variation of local contact potential difference. LCPD maps were fitted to parabolic expressions of frequency shift. Data was collected on a 64 x 80 pixel grid. Theoretical calculations used DFT methods in the FHI-AIMS code. The PBE version of GGA was employed for exchange-correlation. SAPT0 analysis was performed using the PSI4 program.

Procedures And Architectures
STM topography was acquired in constant current mode. nc-AFM imaging operated in frequency modulation mode. Oscillation amplitude for nc-AFM was set to 200 pm. KPFM images were captured in constant height mode. The tip-sample height was chosen near Δf minima. This choice ensures the absence of tip relaxation. KPFM simulations used the PP-AFM code. Simulated images matched experimental evidence well. DFT calculations used a 4-layer Au(111) slab. The surface supercell corresponded to a 6×6 unit cell. Van der Waals correction used Tkatchenko-Scheffler method. Geometries were optimized when forces were under 2 meV/Å. The CO tip termination had a charge quadrupole of -0.2 e/Å². SAPT0 cluster models used a single layer of 38 gold atoms.

Key Results
FCl-An and An formed ordered molecular islands on Au(111). The supramolecular assembly has a rhombic periodic structure. The unit cell contains one An and two FCl-An molecules. KPFM revealed a bow-tie pattern in FCl-An molecules. This pattern corresponds to the π-hole charge distribution. Anthracene molecules did not exhibit this submolecular contrast. Force-distance spectroscopy showed a 30 pm difference in minima. The adsorption height of An was determined to be 330 pm. The adsorption height of FCl-An was determined to be 360 pm. FCl-An adsorbs higher than An on the Au(111) surface. DFT calculations confirmed these adsorption heights reasonably well. Induced electron density was higher for An than FCl-An. SAPT0 analysis showed induction energy is larger for An. The π-hole increases the ionization potential of FCl-An.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The π-hole creates a positive electrostatic potential in the center. This affects non-covalent intermolecular interactions significantly. The π-hole increases the ionization potential of the molecule. Higher ionization potential inhibits charge density induction. Weaker induced electrostatic interactions result in larger adsorption height. The study confirms the theoretical prediction of π-hole existence. It demonstrates the importance of submolecular charge distribution. KPFM is validated as a tool for real-space charge mapping. The findings expand understanding of π-hole systems. It opens possibilities for studying chemical properties influenced by charge.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The study compared FCl-An with anthracene as a control. KPFM simulations were compared with experimental data. SAPT0 and DFT calculations gave similar adsorption energies. The effect of tip-sample distance was analyzed.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 illustrates the charge distribution in PAHs. Figure 2 shows the molecular self-assembly structure. Figure 3 presents KPFM images and simulations. Figure 4 displays force-distance spectroscopy and induced density. Table S2 presents adsorption energies from DFT and SAPT0. Table S3 presents SAPT0 energy decomposition.
